title: What Is Inflation?
paragraphs: Inflation seldom announces itself; rather, it insinuates itself into daily life, in the creeping cost of groceries, in rising rents, in the quiet sense that a fixed income no longer stretches as far as it once did. Economists define it as a sustained increase in the general price level, and because it governs the purchasing power of every household and enterprise, it is among the most intensely scrutinised measures of economic health.

Fundamentally, inflation erodes the real value of money. Where nominal wages stagnate as prices advance, living standards decline and cash savings are steadily hollowed out. To quantify the phenomenon, national statistical agencies compile a consumer price index, charting the cost of a representative basket of goods and services, spanning food, energy, housing and transport, against its level twelve months earlier.

Its origins are conventionally divided into two broad categories. Demand-pull inflation emerges when aggregate expenditure outpaces the economy's productive capacity, emboldening sellers to raise prices; cost-push inflation, conversely, originates on the supply side, as abrupt increases in the cost of energy, raw materials or labour are transmitted to consumers. An unduly rapid expansion of the money supply may compound either dynamic.

Stewardship of price stability ordinarily falls to an independent central bank, many of which pursue an inflation target in the region of two percent per annum. Their foremost instrument is the policy interest rate: by raising it, they render borrowing costlier and saving more remunerative, thereby restraining demand. The transmission of such measures is, however, protracted, frequently requiring many months to register in consumer prices.
